hook.text: In 1720, the South Sea Company promised investors riches from trade. Its stock rose 800% before crashing to nothing.

buildup.text: The British government let the company take over national debt.

discovery.text: The company had almost no real trade revenue. The stock price was pure speculation fed by insider manipulation.

twist.text: Isaac Newton invested early, sold for a profit, then reinvested near the peak and lost £20,000 — a fortune at the time.

climax.text: Even a genius couldn't resist the bubble. The South Sea crash proved that herd behavior defeats individual intelligence.

punchline.text: Newton lost a fortune. The South Sea Bubble defeated even genius.

quiz.question: What happened to Isaac Newton during the South Sea Bubble?
options: He sold at a profit then reinvested near the peak and lost £20,000

hook.text: Overend Gurney was London's biggest discount bank. On May 10, 1866.

buildup.text: The bank had lent recklessly to railway speculators and shipbuilders. When loans went bad, losses exceeded capital.

discovery.text: Depositors rushed to withdraw. The Bank of England refused to bail them out.

twist.text: This crisis established the lender of last resort principle.

climax.text: One bank's failure reshaped central banking. Overend Gurney's collapse created the modern lender of last resort concept.

punchline.text: The Bank of England refused to help. 200 firms failed.

quiz.question: What principle did the Overend Gurney collapse establish?
options: The lender of last resort concept

hook.text: Two speculators tried to corner the copper market in 1907. When they failed, the banks that funded them collapsed.

buildup.text: Trust companies had lent heavily to the speculators. When Knickerbocker Trust failed.

discovery.text: J.P. Morgan organized a rescue. He locked bankers in his library until they agreed to pool funds and stop the panic.

twist.text: Morgan profited from the rescue by buying assets at distressed prices. The savior was also the biggest winner.

climax.text: One private banker saving the financial system proved the need for a central bank.

punchline.text: Morgan saved the system and profited from it.

quiz.question: What did the Panic of 1907 lead to?
options: The creation of the Federal Reserve

hook.text: In 1930, the Bank of United States failed. Despite its name, it was a private bank.

buildup.text: The bank's directors had made risky real estate loans and manipulated the bank's stock price to hide losses.

discovery.text: It was the largest bank failure in American history at the time. The FDIC didn't exist yet — deposits had no protection.

twist.text: Other banks refused to rescue it because its customers were mostly Jewish immigrants.

climax.text: The failure deepened the Great Depression in New York. Fear spread to every bank, accelerating bank runs nationwide.

punchline.text: 400,000 depositors lost everything. No FDIC. No rescue. Fear spread nationwide.

quiz.question: Why did other banks refuse to rescue the Bank of United States?
options: Bias against its predominantly immigrant customers

hook.text: Crédit Mobilier was a construction company that bribed Congress.

buildup.text: The company overbilled Union Pacific Railroad by $44 million for construction. Insiders kept the difference as profit.

discovery.text: To avoid investigation, Crédit Mobilier gave shares to US congressmen. The bribery reached the Vice President himself.

twist.text: When exposed in 1872, public trust in both banking and government collapsed.

climax.text: Crédit Mobilier showed that banking fraud and political corruption feed each other. Money buys silence and immunity.

punchline.text: $44 million stolen. Congress bribed. Nobody went to prison.

quiz.question: How did Crédit Mobilier avoid investigation?
options: By giving shares to members of Congress

hook.text: Between 1930 and 1933, 9,000 US banks failed. One in three banks vanished. Millions of families lost their life savings.

buildup.text: Banks had invested deposits in the stock market. When stocks crashed 86%, banks couldn't return their depositors' money.

discovery.text: Bank runs are self-fulfilling. When people fear a bank will fail, they rush to withdraw.

twist.text: FDR's bank holiday in 1933 closed every bank for four days. Only solvent banks were allowed to reopen.

climax.text: The mass failure created the FDIC. Deposit insurance guaranteed $2,500 per account and ended panic withdrawals.

punchline.text: 9,000 banks failed. FDR created deposit insurance. Bank runs largely stopped.

quiz.question: What ended the Depression-era bank run cycle?

topics.title: Continental Illinois: Too Big to Fail

hook.text: In 1984, Continental Illinois was America's seventh-largest bank. It failed in what regulators called 'too big to fail.'

buildup.text: The bank had bought $1 billion in risky oil and gas loans from Penn Square Bank.

discovery.text: Electronic bank runs arrived. Continental lost $10 billion in deposits via wire transfers in days, not weeks.

twist.text: The FDIC rescued every depositor, even those above the $100,000 insurance limit.

climax.text: Continental Illinois created the moral hazard problem: big banks get rescued, small banks don't.

punchline.text: Too big to fail. The phrase and the problem were born with Continental Illinois.

quiz.question: What term was coined during the Continental Illinois failure?

topics.title: Penn Square Bank: Small Bank, Big Damage

hook.text: Penn Square Bank was a tiny Oklahoma shopping mall bank.

buildup.text: Penn Square wrote massive energy loans and sold them to bigger banks.

discovery.text: The loans were poorly underwritten. Penn Square's loan officers approved deals on napkins.

twist.text: When Penn Square failed in 1982, the losses cascaded upward.

climax.text: A small bank in a strip mall originated loans that toppled giants. Size doesn't determine systemic risk; connections do.

punchline.text: A shopping mall bank. Loans on napkins. It nearly crashed the system.

quiz.question: Why was Penn Square Bank's failure so damaging?
options: It had sold risky loans to larger banks that also failed

hook.text: 1,043 savings and loan banks failed between 1986 and 1995. The government bailout cost taxpayers $132 billion.

buildup.text: S&Ls were community banks that took savings and made home loans.

discovery.text: With deposits insured by the government, S&L owners gambled freely. If they won, they kept profits.

twist.text: Charles Keating bribed five US senators to delay his S&L's investigation.

climax.text: The S&L crisis proved that deposit insurance without regulation creates moral hazard.

punchline.text: 1,043 banks failed. $132 billion taxpayer bailout.

quiz.question: How many S&L institutions failed during the crisis?

hook.text: Five US senators accepted $1.3 million from banker Charles Keating.

buildup.text: Keating ran Lincoln Savings and Loan. He used depositors' money on junk bonds and luxury real estate projects.

discovery.text: When regulators investigated, Keating called his senators. They held a meeting pressuring the regulators to back off.

twist.text: Lincoln Savings collapsed in 1989. 23,000 depositors lost savings. Keating went to prison.

climax.text: The Keating Five showed how money buys political protection for bad banking.

punchline.text: $1.3 million in donations. Five senators pressured regulators.

quiz.question: What did the five senators do for Charles Keating?
options: Pressured regulators to stop investigating his S&L

hook.text: Nick Leeson was a 28-year-old trader who single-handedly destroyed Britain's oldest merchant bank. Barings fell in 1995.

buildup.text: Leeson was supposed to make safe arbitrage trades in Singapore. Instead he made massive bets on Japanese stock futures.

discovery.text: He hid losses in a secret account numbered 88888. By the time anyone found out, losses exceeded $1.3 billion.

twist.text: Barings had survived 233 years, financed wars, and served the Queen. One trader in a back office wiped it all out.

climax.text: Barings' failure proved that internal controls matter more than reputation.

punchline.text: 233-year-old bank. One rogue trader. $1.3 billion in hidden losses. Gone.

quiz.question: How did Nick Leeson hide his trading losses?

hook.text: LTCM was run by Nobel Prize winners. Their hedge fund nearly crashed the global financial system in 1998.

buildup.text: LTCM used mathematical models to find tiny price differences in bond markets.

discovery.text: Russia's debt default in 1998 caused market turmoil their models didn't predict. LTCM lost $4.6 billion in four months.

twist.text: The Fed organized a $3.6 billion rescue by 14 banks. Taxpayer money wasn't used.

climax.text: Nobel Prize models failed because markets aren't purely mathematical.

punchline.text: Nobel Prize winners. 25:1 leverage. $4.6 billion lost in four months.

quiz.question: Why did LTCM's models fail?
options: They couldn't account for extreme events like Russia's default

hook.text: In 1997, Thailand's currency collapsed overnight. Within months.

buildup.text: Asian banks had borrowed heavily in US dollars to fund local real estate.

discovery.text: Thailand, Indonesia, and South Korea all needed IMF bailouts. Indonesia's banking sector lost 80% of its value.

twist.text: The IMF demanded austerity in exchange for bailouts. Spending cuts deepened the recession.

climax.text: The Asian crisis showed that currency pegs and foreign debt are a dangerous combination.

punchline.text: Currency collapsed. Dollar debts exploded. Asia's banks fell like dominoes.

quiz.question: What made Asian bank debts so dangerous in 1997?
options: They borrowed in US dollars while earning local currencies

hook.text: Japan's real estate bubble burst in 1990. Banks held trillions in bad loans but hid them for a decade.

buildup.text: At the peak, Tokyo's Imperial Palace grounds were worth more than all California real estate. Then prices collapsed 80%.

discovery.text: Japanese banks practiced 'extend and pretend.' They renewed bad loans instead of writing them off.

twist.text: Japan's GDP stayed near zero for two decades. The banking system's refusal to recognize losses froze the economy.

climax.text: Japan proved that hiding banking losses delays recovery.

punchline.text: Hide the losses. Fund the zombies. Japan's economy froze for 20 years.

quiz.question: What are 'zombie banks'?
options: Banks that keep renewing bad loans instead of recognizing losses

hook.text: BCCI operated in 78 countries and laundered money for drug cartels, terrorists, and dictators.

buildup.text: Founded in 1972, BCCI grew rapidly by offering unusually high returns.

discovery.text: BCCI was a Ponzi scheme. New deposits paid old depositors' returns.

twist.text: BCCI bribed politicians and regulators in multiple countries.

climax.text: When BCCI collapsed in 1991, $20 billion disappeared. It proved that global banks need global oversight.

punchline.text: 78 countries. Drug money. Arms deals. $20 billion gone.

quiz.question: Why was BCCI able to operate corruptly for so long?
options: It was too small to notice
Operating across 78 countries meant no single regulator could see everything

topics.title: Bear Stearns: The First to Fall

hook.text: In March 2008, Bear Stearns collapsed in 72 hours. The fifth-largest US investment bank was sold for $2 per share.

buildup.text: Bear Stearns was heavily exposed to subprime mortgage securities.

discovery.text: Counterparties refused to trade with Bear. Without trust, an investment bank cannot operate.

twist.text: JPMorgan bought Bear Stearns for $2 per share with Fed backing. A year earlier, shares traded at $170.

climax.text: Bear Stearns proved that investment banks die from loss of confidence, not loss of capital.

punchline.text: $170 to $2 per share in one year. Trust collapsed before the capital did.

quiz.question: Why did Bear Stearns collapse so quickly?
options: Counterparties lost trust and refused to trade with them

topics.title: Lehman Brothers: The Crash Heard Worldwide

hook.text: On September 15, 2008, Lehman Brothers filed for bankruptcy. $639 billion in assets vanished.

buildup.text: Lehman held massive positions in mortgage-backed securities.

discovery.text: The government decided not to bail out Lehman. Officials believed the market could absorb the failure.

twist.text: The money market fund Reserve Primary broke the buck because of Lehman exposure.

climax.text: Lehman's failure proved that one bankruptcy can crash the world economy.

punchline.text: $639 billion bankruptcy. The world economy nearly collapsed in 48 hours.

quiz.question: What happened when the government let Lehman Brothers fail?
options: Global financial panic spread within hours

topics.title: AIG: The Insurance Company That Almost Killed Banking

hook.text: AIG sold $440 billion in credit default swaps — insurance on mortgage bonds.

buildup.text: Banks bought CDS from AIG to hedge their mortgage risk.

discovery.text: AIG needed $185 billion from the government. Without the bailout.

twist.text: Days after the bailout, AIG paid $165 million in executive bonuses.

climax.text: AIG proved that insurance companies can create systemic banking risk.

punchline.text: $440 billion in insurance. $185 billion bailout. Then executive bonuses.

quiz.question: What made AIG's failure so dangerous to the banking system?
options: Banks relied on AIG's credit default swaps as insurance against mortgage losses

topics.title: Washington Mutual: Largest Bank Failure Ever

hook.text: Washington Mutual was the largest bank failure in US history. $307 billion in assets collapsed in September 2008.

buildup.text: WaMu aggressively sold subprime mortgages. Loan officers were paid bonuses based on volume, not quality.

discovery.text: Depositors withdrew $16.7 billion in 10 days. The FDIC seized the bank and sold it to JPMorgan for $1.9 billion.

twist.text: WaMu's CEO Kerry Killinger received $25 million in compensation the year before the bank failed.

climax.text: WaMu proved that volume-based lending incentives create fraud. When you pay for quantity, quality disappears.

punchline.text: $307 billion gone. The CEO earned $25 million the year before collapse.

quiz.question: What made Washington Mutual's lending so risky?
options: Loan officers were paid bonuses based on volume, not quality

hook.text: Iceland's three largest banks grew to 10 times the nation's GDP.

buildup.text: Icelandic banks offered high-interest online savings accounts across Europe.

discovery.text: Total banking assets reached $182 billion for a country with 330,000 people.

twist.text: Iceland let its banks fail and prosecuted 26 bankers. It recovered faster than countries that bailed out their banks.

climax.text: Iceland proved that banking sectors can outgrow their countries.

punchline.text: Banks 10x the GDP. Iceland let them fail and recovered faster than expected.

quiz.question: How did Iceland respond to its banking collapse?
options: Let banks fail and prosecuted bankers

hook.text: Silicon Valley Bank collapsed in 48 hours in March 2023.

buildup.text: SVB invested deposits in long-term government bonds. When the Fed raised rates, those bonds lost $15 billion in value.

discovery.text: 96% of SVB deposits were above the $250,000 FDIC insurance limit. Tech startups held millions per account.

twist.text: The FDIC stepped in and guaranteed ALL deposits, even uninsured ones.

climax.text: SVB was the first social media bank run. Twitter and group chats spread panic faster than any 1930s headline could.

punchline.text: $42 billion in one day. The first bank run driven by apps and tweets.

quiz.question: What percentage of SVB deposits were above the FDIC insurance limit?

hook.text: Credit Suisse survived two world wars and multiple crises. In 2023, it collapsed and was absorbed by rival UBS.

buildup.text: Years of scandals eroded trust: Archegos losses, Greensill exposure, money laundering fines.

discovery.text: Customers withdrew $119 billion in the fourth quarter of 2022 alone. For a bank, customer flight is a death sentence.

twist.text: The Swiss government forced UBS to buy Credit Suisse over a weekend.

climax.text: Credit Suisse proved that reputation is a bank's most valuable asset.

punchline.text: 167 years old. $119 billion withdrawn. Absorbed by a rival in a weekend.

quiz.question: What ultimately caused Credit Suisse's downfall?
options: Years of scandals that destroyed customer trust

topics.title: Signature Bank and the Crypto Connection

hook.text: Signature Bank failed in March 2023, two days after SVB. It had become the banking partner for crypto firms.

buildup.text: Signature embraced crypto deposits when other banks wouldn't. Its Signet platform let crypto companies move money 24/7.

discovery.text: When crypto markets crashed and FTX collapsed, Signature lost billions in deposits.

twist.text: Regulators seized Signature before depositors could run.

climax.text: Signature showed that new industries bring new risks. Serving crypto clients made a bank vulnerable to crypto crises.

punchline.text: Embraced crypto. Crypto crashed. The bank failed two days after SVB.

quiz.question: What made Signature Bank uniquely vulnerable?
options: Heavy dependence on cryptocurrency industry deposits

topics.title: First Republic Bank: The Wealth Bank

hook.text: First Republic catered to wealthy clients in San Francisco and New York.

buildup.text: First Republic offered jumbo mortgages at below-market rates to attract wealthy depositors.

discovery.text: When SVB failed, wealthy depositors panicked and pulled $100 billion from First Republic despite reassurances.

twist.text: 11 major banks deposited $30 billion to rescue First Republic. It wasn't enough.

climax.text: First Republic proved that even serving the wealthy doesn't prevent bank runs.

punchline.text: Served the wealthy. Lost $100 billion in deposits.

quiz.question: What happened to the $30 billion rescue deposit for First Republic?
options: It wasn't enough, and JPMorgan acquired the bank anyway

hook.text: Wirecard was a German fintech darling worth $28 billion.

buildup.text: Wirecard processed payments for online merchants. It claimed rapid growth in Asia.

discovery.text: The $2.1 billion was supposedly held in Philippine bank accounts. The banks confirmed the accounts didn't exist.

twist.text: Germany's financial regulator BaFin had investigated whistleblowers who reported fraud.

climax.text: Wirecard proved that regulators can be fooled by national champions.

punchline.text: $2.1 billion that never existed. Regulators investigated whistleblowers instead.

quiz.question: What was unique about Wirecard's fraud?
options: $2.1 billion in reported cash simply did not exist in any account
It was only detected by AI

hook.text: Banks have failed for 4,000 years. The causes repeat: excess leverage, risky bets, fraud, and loss of public confidence.

buildup.text: Every banking crisis follows a pattern: innovation, euphoria, over-lending, then collapse. The cycle never breaks.

discovery.text: Humans are wired for short-term thinking. Bankers optimize for this quarter's profit, not the next decade's stability.

twist.text: Regulations written after each crisis get weakened during the next boom. Memory fades, rules relax, and risk returns.

climax.text: Banking failures are systemic, not accidental. The incentive structure rewards risk-taking until the system breaks.

punchline.text: Same causes for 4,000 years. Leverage, risk, fraud, and lost trust.

quiz.question: Why do banking crises keep repeating?
options: Structural incentives reward risk-taking, and regulations weaken over time

hook.text: FDIC insurance ended bank runs but created moral hazard. Depositors stopped checking if their bank was safe.

buildup.text: Before FDIC, depositors closely watched their bank's health. Insurance removed the incentive to monitor bank behavior.

discovery.text: Banks take bigger risks because insured depositors don't flee. Only uninsured depositors create market discipline.

twist.text: SVB proved the limits. 96% uninsured deposits created massive run risk that insurance wasn't designed to cover.

climax.text: Deposit insurance is essential but imperfect. It prevents panic at the cost of reducing accountability.

punchline.text: Stops bank runs. But removes the incentive for depositors to watch their bank.

quiz.question: What is the downside of deposit insurance?
options: It reduces depositors' incentive to monitor bank health

hook.text: In the 1930s, bank runs took weeks. Continental Illinois took days. SVB took hours. Speed is getting faster.

buildup.text: Digital banking lets depositors move billions instantly. There's no line at the door — just a button on a phone.

discovery.text: Social media amplifies panic. A single tweet can trigger $42 billion in withdrawals before regulators even respond.

twist.text: Regulators still operate at 1930s speed. By the time they hold a meeting, the bank is already gone.

climax.text: Technology made banking faster but also made failure faster.

punchline.text: Weeks to days to hours. Bank failures now happen at app speed.

quiz.question: How has technology changed bank failures?
options: Dramatically increased the speed of bank runs

hook.text: Bank failures cost someone money. The question is always who: shareholders, depositors, other banks, or taxpayers.

buildup.text: The FDIC fund is paid by bank premiums. When failures exceed the fund.

discovery.text: In 2008, taxpayers funded $700 billion through TARP. In 2023.

twist.text: Banks pass their FDIC premiums to customers through lower rates and higher fees. Customers always pay in the end.

climax.text: The cost of bank failures is always shared across the economy. The only question is how visibly and how fairly.

punchline.text: Shareholders lose first. Taxpayers bail out last. Customers pay through fees.

quiz.question: How are FDIC premiums ultimately funded?
options: Banks pay premiums but pass costs to customers through fees

topics.title: Can We Prevent the Next Failure?

hook.text: After every bank failure, politicians say 'never again.' After every boom, they weaken the rules they wrote.

buildup.text: Glass-Steagall lasted 66 years. Dodd-Frank was weakened within 8.

discovery.text: Better regulation helps but can't eliminate risk. Banking requires maturity transformation, which is inherently fragile.

twist.text: The banking industry spends $700 million annually lobbying Congress. The biggest spenders are the biggest banks.

climax.text: Banking failures can be reduced but not eliminated. The system is designed to take risks.

punchline.text: $700 million in lobbying. The cycle of crisis and reform will never end.

quiz.question: How much does the banking industry spend on lobbying annually?
